items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
鶏肉とたまねぎを米と一緒に炊き込むだけの、飾らない一皿。使う調味料は醤油と砂糖と酒だけで、余計な香りを足さない分、鶏の出汁の旨みがまっすぐ伝わってくる。炊き上がった米粒はあめ色につやつやと光り、噛むほどに鶏の風味と香ばしさが広がるという。どの家庭も使う食材はほぼ同じだが、味付けの配分は家庭ごとに違う、いわば手加減の郷土料理でもある。
## どう作るのか
鶏もも肉とむね肉を油で炒め、調味料で下味をつけたあと、たまねぎを加えてシャキシャキ感が残る程度にさっと煮る。具と煮汁をざるで分けたら、煮汁とバター、米を炊飯器に入れて炊き上げ、最後に炊けたごはんへ具を混ぜ込んで仕上げる。米に対して具はごくわずかで、シンプルな調理だからこそ鶏の出汁の旨みがそのまま前面に出るという。地域によってはラーメンと合わせて食べる風習も伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
明治の開拓期、美唄市中村地区に入植した農場主が、稲作が軌道にのるまでの間、小作人たちの暮らしを案じてつがいの鶏を分け与え、養鶏を勧めたのが始まりと伝わる。米がとれるようになると、客をもてなすために鶏をつぶし、米と一緒に炊き込んで振る舞ったという。いまも中村地区では地元の女性たちが、昔ながらの味を毎朝炊き上げて受け継いでいる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
A plain, unadorned dish of chicken and onion simmered right into the rice. The seasoning is just soy sauce, sugar, and sake — nothing more — so the savor of the chicken stock comes through unmasked. The finished rice grains are said to glisten amber, releasing more chicken flavor and a faint toastiness with every bite. Every household uses roughly the same ingredients, yet the balance of seasoning differs from kitchen to kitchen — a home-cooked dish measured by feel.
## How it's made
Chicken thigh and breast are pan-fried in oil, seasoned, then simmered briefly with onion so it keeps some crunch. The solids are strained from the broth, and the broth goes into a rice cooker with butter and rice; once it's cooked, the chicken and onion are folded back into the finished rice. The meat is a small share against the rice, and that restraint is said to be exactly what lets the chicken stock carry the dish. In some areas, it is said to be eaten alongside a bowl of ramen.
## Why it took this shape
During the Meiji-era settlement of Hokkaido, a farm owner who had taken up land in the Nakamura district of Bibai is said to have given tenant farmers pairs of chickens to raise, worried about their livelihood before the rice paddies came into their own. Once rice finally came in, he is said to have slaughtered the chickens he kept and served this rice dish to welcome guests. Local women in Nakamura still carry the tradition on, cooking the dish fresh each morning.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
秋から冬にとれる鮭と、キャベツやたまねぎ、人参、ピーマン、もやしといった旬の野菜を、味噌とバターで一気に蒸し焼きにする。鉄板の上で味噌が焦げる香ばしい匂いが真っ先に立ち、脂の乗った鮭の身に野菜の甘みがからむ。一品で食卓が豪華になるうえ野菜もたっぷり摂れることから、幅広い世代に好まれてきたという。仕上げにマヨネーズをかけて食べる若い世代も多いと伝わる。
## どう作るのか
三枚におろした鮭とバター、季節の野菜を鉄板にのせ、味噌と砂糖、みりん、酒で味付けしながら蒸し焼きにする。伝統的には漁師町らしくドラム缶を鉄板代わりにして焼いていたと伝わり、いまはホットプレートやホイル焼きでもつくられる。家庭で手早くつくれるよう切り身の鮭を使うことも多く、調理の道具立ては時代とともに変わっても、蒸し焼きという核だけは変わっていないという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
石狩地方の漁師町で、船の上や浜辺で手早く仕上げていた食べ方が始まりと伝わる。名前の由来には諸説あり、「ちゃっちゃとつくれるから」「お父ちゃんがつくるから」「鉄板とヘラがチャンチャンと音を立てるから」など、いずれも漁師の暮らしの手早さを映した説として語り継がれている。サケの漁獲量が国内でも際立って多い土地だからこその一皿といえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Salmon caught between autumn and winter is pan-steamed all at once with cabbage, onion, carrot, green pepper, and bean sprouts in miso and butter. The first thing that hits you is the smell of miso browning on the griddle, and the fatty salmon carries the sweetness of the vegetables with it. A single pan makes for a hearty spread and packs in plenty of vegetables, which is said to be why it appeals across generations. Many younger eaters are said to finish it with a squeeze of mayonnaise.
## How it's made
Salmon filleted into three pieces is laid on a griddle with butter and seasonal vegetables, then pan-steamed while seasoned with miso, sugar, mirin, and sake. Fishing-town tradition is said to have used an old oil-drum griddle set up right on the shore; today it's more often made on a hot plate or wrapped in foil. Many households use salmon fillets instead of a whole fish for the sake of speed — the tools have changed with the times, but the pan-steaming at its core has not.
## Why it took this shape
It's said to trace back to fishing towns in the Ishikari region, where it was cooked quickly on deck or right on the beach. The name's origin has several tellings — that it could be made in a hurry ("chatcha"), that "chan" was what the father of the house was called, or that it imitates the clang of spatula on iron griddle — each one said to echo the brisk pace of a fisherman's life. It's a dish that could only come from a place with one of Japan's largest salmon catches.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
上新粉に白砂糖と黒砂糖をそれぞれ混ぜた生地を木の葉の形に整えて蒸す、白と黒の二色使いが定番の菓子。もっちりと柔らかい食感とほどよい甘さで、子どもから大人まで懐かしい味として親しまれているという。道南地域を中心に、黒糖だけの単色やよもぎを混ぜた緑色、花形や丸形など、彩りも形もさまざまなべこ餅がいまも各地でつくられている。
## どう作るのか
上新粉と砂糖を混ぜ合わせて生地をつくり、白い生地には白砂糖、黒い生地には黒砂糖を練り込んで蒸し上げる。木型を使って木の葉形に仕上げるのが昔ながらのやり方だが、木型を使わずに手で形をととのえる家庭や店もある。以前は木型を持つ家庭も多く、行事のたびに親子で手づくりしていたと伝わる。多くつくりすぎたときは冷凍しておけば日持ちするという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
発祥には諸説あり、山形県の郷土菓子「くじら餅」が北海道で独自に進化して木の葉形になったとも伝わり、道南地域の一部ではいまも「くじら餅」と呼ぶ地域がある。名前の由来も、白と黒の配色が牛（べこ）を連想させるという説、黒糖の色が「べっこう」に近いという説、米粉（べいこ）が転じたという説など諸説語られる。北海道では端午の節句によく食べられ、正月や彼岸、冠婚葬祭などハレの日にも供されてきたという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Rice flour dough mixed separately with white and brown sugar is shaped into leaves and steamed, the white-and-black pairing being the classic look. The texture is soft and chewy with a gentle sweetness, said to be a nostalgic flavor loved by children and adults alike. Mostly in the Donan region, versions also turn up today in solid brown sugar, in mugwort green, or shaped as flowers and circles instead of leaves.
## How it's made
Rice flour is mixed with sugar into dough, white sugar for the white dough and brown sugar for the black, then it's steamed. The traditional method presses the dough into a leaf shape with a wooden mold, though some households and shops simply shape it by hand instead. Many families are said to have once owned their own wooden mold, making it together at home for each seasonal occasion. Made in a big batch, it's said to keep well if frozen.
## Why it took this shape
Its origins carry more than one telling — one holds that Yamagata's kujira-mochi confection evolved independently in Hokkaido into this leaf shape, and part of the Donan region still calls it "kujira-mochi" today. The name itself has several stories too: that the black-and-white coloring recalls a Holstein cow (beko), that the brown sugar's hue resembles tortoiseshell (bekko), or that it comes from rice flour (beiko). In Hokkaido it has long been eaten around the Boys' Festival in May, and it is also said to appear at New Year, the equinox, and other formal family occasions.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
蒸してつぶしたじゃがいもに片栗粉を混ぜ、焼き目がつくまで焼くだけの軽食。地域によっては「いもだんご」とも呼ばれる。男爵いもでつくられることが多く、外はかりっと香ばしく、中はもちもちとした食感が持ち味とされる。バターをのせたり、甘辛いごまダレをつけたりと、食べ方は家庭や地域によってさまざまという。通年出回るじゃがいもを使うため、季節を問わず食べられている。
## どう作るのか
蒸したじゃがいもをつぶし、まんじゅう状にととのえたら、あとは焦げ目がつくまで焼く。片栗粉だけでもつくれるが、小麦粉を少し加えると口当たりがなめらかになるという。チーズを中に入れて焼いたり、揚げたり、汁物に入れたりと、家庭によってさまざまなアレンジが加えられ、同じ食材からいくつもの食べ方が枝分かれしている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
稲作の生産技術がまだ発達していなかった時代、餅をつくる際にもち米の代わりに、当時すでに豊富に生産されていたじゃがいもを使ったのが始まりと伝わる。明治の開拓期には貴重なエネルギー源として重宝され、その手軽さから庶民の料理として広まっていった。戦時中や戦後の食糧難の時代にも食べられ続け、じゃがいもの代わりにかぼちゃを使う「かぼちゃもち」も、いまに伝わっている。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Steamed potato is mashed, bound with potato starch, and pan-fried until browned — a simple snack also called imodango in some areas. It's most often made with danshaku potatoes, and the appeal is said to lie in the crisp, toasty outside against a soft, chewy inside. Butter on top, or a sweet-savory sesame sauce — how it's eaten varies by household and region, and since potatoes are sold year-round, so is the snack itself.
## How it's made
Steamed potato is mashed, shaped into small patties, and pan-fried until it browns. Potato starch alone will bind it, but a little wheat flour added in is said to make the texture smoother. Households vary it further — stuffing it with cheese before frying, deep-frying it, or dropping it into soup — so that a single ingredient branches into several different ways of eating.
## Why it took this shape
In an era before rice-growing technology had taken hold locally, potato — already grown in abundance — is said to have stood in for glutinous rice when making mochi, and that's how this began. During the Meiji-era settlement it served as a vital source of energy, and its simplicity to make helped it spread as an everyday, working people's food. It kept being eaten through the wartime and postwar years of rice shortage, and a pumpkin version made the same way, kabocha-mochi, is also still passed down today.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
ニシンやホッケ、サケなど北海道でとれる魚と、キャベツや人参、大根、しょうがといった野菜を、米麹と一緒に低温でじっくり乳酸発酵させたなれずし。ほかのなれずしに比べて漬け込む期間が短いため、匂いはおだやかとされる。米の甘みと乳酸の酸っぱさのバランスがよく、食事としても酒の肴としても好まれるという。とりわけ手ごろで通年安定して獲れるホッケが使われることが多い。
## どう作るのか
かために炊いて冷ました米と、新鮮な魚、野菜、麹を混ぜて樽に入れ、重石をのせて漬け込み発酵させる。塩漬けにした生魚は水で塩抜きしてから使うが、この加減が味を決めるといえるほど大事な作業とされる。抜きすぎれば味も保存も効かず、足りなければ塩辛くなりすぎてしまうという。魚と米、麹の重なりを樽の中でじっと待つ、時間そのものが調味料になる料理ともいえる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
初雪が降るころ、漁師の家でつくられていたのが発祥とされ、低温発酵という製法自体、北海道から東北にかけての気温の低い沿岸部だからこそ根づいたと伝わる。晩秋に漬け込んで正月ごろに食べる、冬の伝統的な保存食として地域に定着してきた。地域ごとにつくり方が微妙に異なるのも、各地の漁師町で独自に育まれてきたことの表れといえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
A narezushi made by slow, cold lactic fermentation of Hokkaido-caught fish — herring, atka mackerel, salmon — layered with rice malt and vegetables like cabbage, carrot, daikon, and ginger. It's said to smell milder than other narezushi styles because the fermentation period is shorter. The rice's sweetness balances against the malt's sourness in a way that suits it equally to a meal or a drink. Atka mackerel is especially common, being affordable and caught steadily through the year.
## How it's made
Rice cooked firm and cooled is mixed with fresh fish, vegetables, and malt, packed into a barrel, and weighted down to ferment. The salted raw fish is first soaked in water to draw out the salt, and getting that step right is said to make or break the dish — too little salt removed and it won't keep or taste of much, too much and it turns overly salty. It's a dish where fish, rice, and malt simply sit together in the barrel, and time itself does the seasoning.
## Why it took this shape
It's said to have begun in fishing households around the time of the first snowfall, and the cold-fermentation method itself is said to have taken root precisely because of the cold coastal climate running from Hokkaido down into Tohoku. Packed in late autumn and eaten around New Year, it settled into the region as a traditional winter preserve. That each area's recipe differs slightly is itself a sign of how each fishing town shaped it in its own way.

sources.title: 飯寿司 北海道 | うちの郷土料理：農林水産省
sources.publisher: 農林水産省「うちの郷土料理」

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
羊肉を、たまねぎやもやし、ピーマン、とうもろこしといった野菜と一緒に専用の鍋で焼く料理。使われる羊肉は、臭みの少ない生後1年未満の「ラム」と、脂がのってしっかりした味わいの生後2年以上の「マトン」の二種類。生のまま焼いてタレにつけるものと、あらかじめ醤油ベースのタレに漬け込んだ味付きのものと、食べ方も二通りある。
## どう作るのか
中央が盛り上がり、まわりに溝のある独特の形をした鍋を使う。肉を中央の盛り上がった部分で焼くと、肉汁が溝を伝って外側の野菜に流れ落ち、野菜に味がじんわりと染み込んでいく。北海道の家庭にはこの専用鍋を持つところが多く、春の花見や夏のバーベキューなど、屋外で仲間と囲む食べ方も定着しているという。一緒に焼く野菜の組み合わせは家庭ごとに違うとも伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
大正期、第一次世界大戦で羊毛の輸入が難しくなったことを背景に、国策として綿羊の飼育が奨励され、北海道でも盛んになったのが羊肉を食べる習慣の始まりと伝わる。発祥には諸説あるが、当時羊肉を食べる習慣のなかった日本人向けに、中国料理の羊の焼肉を参考に考案されたともいわれる。溝のある鍋の形そのものが、羊肉特有の脂と臭みを野菜の下へ落とし、旨みだけを行き渡らせる工夫として読み解ける。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Lamb or mutton is grilled together with vegetables — onion, bean sprouts, green pepper, corn — on a dedicated grill pan. Two kinds of meat are used: lamb from animals under a year old, milder in smell, and mutton from animals two years or older, richer and more assertive in flavor. It's eaten two ways too — grilled plain and dipped in sauce, or pre-marinated in a soy-based sauce before grilling.
## How it's made
The pan itself has a distinctive shape, domed in the center with grooves running down to the rim. Meat grilled on the raised center lets its juices run down the grooves into the vegetables arranged around the edge, slowly soaking them in flavor. Many Hokkaido households are said to own one of these pans, and gathering around it outdoors — for cherry-blossom viewing in spring or a barbecue in summer — has become a fixture of the season. Which vegetables go alongside the meat is said to vary from one household to the next.
## Why it took this shape
During the Taisho era, wool imports grew difficult amid the First World War, and sheep farming was promoted as national policy — Hokkaido took to it too, and that is said to be how eating lamb began here. Its origin carries more than one telling, including that it was devised, for a Japanese public unused to eating lamb, by drawing on a Chinese-style grilled mutton dish. The grooved pan itself can be read as a solution to lamb's particular fat and odor — channeling both away and down into the vegetables, leaving only the savor behind.

sources.title: ジンギスカン 北海道 | うちの郷土料理：農林水産省

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
繊維質が少なく柔らかい日高昆布で、サケやニシンを巻き、かんぴょうで結んで甘辛く煮た一品。昆布の柔らかさゆえに歯切れがよく、魚の身と昆布の旨みが煮汁の醤油と砂糖の甘さに溶け合う。地域や家庭によっては、シシャモやチカの素焼きを昆布で巻くこともあるという。全国トップクラスの生産量を誇る北海道の昆布あってこその料理といえる。
## どう作るのか
昆布とかんぴょうを水で戻し、魚を昆布でくるりと巻いてから、かんぴょうでしっかりと縛る。あとは砂糖、醤油、酒でじっくりと煮含めるだけ。昆布で巻く魚は主にサケかニシンだが、地域や家庭によって使う魚も味付けの濃さもさまざまで、正月の献立にあわせて濃いめに仕上げる家庭も多いという。柔らかい日高昆布だからこそ、巻いてもほどけにくく煮崩れしにくいと伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
北海道は全国の昆布生産量の9割を占める産地で、江戸時代に昆布漁が盛んになると、日本海まわりの「北前船」で本州へと運ばれる主要な積み荷になった。ちょうど同じ時期に漁獲量の多かったニシンや、北海道の名産であるサケと組み合わされ、郷土料理として定着したと伝わる。昆布は「よろこぶ」、ニシンは「二親」の語呂合わせで子孫繁栄や不老長寿を願う縁起物とされ、正月のおせち料理に欠かせない一品になった。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Soft, low-fiber Hidaka kelp is rolled around salmon or herring, tied with a strip of dried gourd, and simmered until sweet and salty. The kelp's softness gives it a clean bite, and the fish's savor melds with the soy-and-sugar sweetness of the broth. In some places, grilled shishamo or Japanese smelt are rolled in kelp instead, a variation only possible thanks to Hokkaido's outsized kelp harvest.
## How it's made
Kelp and dried gourd strips are soaked in water, the fish is rolled up inside a sheet of kelp, and the roll is tied firmly with the gourd strip. From there it's simply simmered slowly in sugar, soy sauce, and sake. Salmon and herring are the usual fillings, but which fish is used and how strong the seasoning runs varies by region and household — many finish it richer for the New Year table. It's the softness of Hidaka kelp that is said to let the roll hold its shape through the simmer without coming undone.
## Why it took this shape
Hokkaido accounts for roughly nine-tenths of Japan's kelp harvest, and once kelp fishing took off in the Edo period, it became a major cargo carried south to Honshu aboard the Kitamaebune ships that sailed the Sea of Japan route. Around the same time, it was paired with herring — then caught in huge numbers — and with Hokkaido's own salmon, and is said to have settled into a local dish from there. Kelp (konbu) puns on "joy" (yorokobu) and herring (nishin) on "two parents," making both auspicious foods wished for descendants and long life, and this dish became a fixture of the New Year's osechi spread.

sources.title: 昆布巻き 北海道 | うちの郷土料理：農林水産省
sources.publisher: 農林水産省「うちの郷土料理」

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
同じ「北海道のラーメン」でも、地域ごとにスープの表情が違う。札幌は味噌、函館は塩、旭川は醤油の上を覆う香味油が特徴とされ、具はねぎやメンマ、チャーシューがオーソドックス。豚骨をベースにした油分の多い濃厚なスープが多く、これはアイヌの人々が食してきた白濁の豚骨スープが受け継がれているという説も伝わる。観光客には特産品を使った味噌バターラーメンや海鮮ラーメンも好まれるという。
## どう作るのか
旭川ではスープの表面を焦がしラードなどの香味油で覆い、湯気を閉じ込めて最後まで熱いまま食べられるように仕立てる。函館は脂分の少ない清湯スープでさっぱりと、釧路は細い縮れ麺で、忙しい漁師にゆで時間を短縮して提供するための工夫と伝わる。道内では自家製麺より製麺所の麺を使う店が多く、店と製麺所の結びつきも深いという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
戦後、気温の低い北海道の食生活にラーメンは急速に浸透し、地域ごとの風土に合わせて工夫が重ねられてきたと伝わる。寒さの厳しい旭川では冷めにくさが、脂の少ない函館では素材の味を生かすさっぱりさが、漁業の街である釧路では手早さが、それぞれの土地の暮らしの必要から生まれた形として読み解ける。地域差の大きさそのものが、この土地の気候と生業の幅を映しているといえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Even under the single label "Hokkaido ramen," the broth wears a different face from city to city — Sapporo's is miso, Hakodate's is salt, and Asahikawa's is soy topped with an aromatic oil. Green onion, bamboo shoots, and roast pork are the standard toppings. The broth often runs rich and fatty, built on pork bone, and one telling holds that this carries forward the cloudy pork-bone stock the Ainu are said to have eaten. Visitors are said to favor versions built on local specialties too, like miso-butter or seafood ramen.
## How it's made
In Asahikawa, the surface of the broth is capped with browned lard or another aromatic oil that traps the steam, keeping the bowl piping hot to the last spoonful. Hakodate favors a clear, low-fat broth for a lighter finish, while Kushiro is known for thin, curly noodles — said to have been a way to cut boiling time for fishermen in a hurry. Most shops on the island use noodles from a noodle maker rather than making their own, and the tie between a shop and its noodle supplier is said to run deep.
## Why it took this shape
After the war, ramen is said to have spread quickly through the diet of cold-climate Hokkaido, with each region layering on its own refinements to suit local conditions. Asahikawa's need to hold heat against the bitter cold, Hakodate's lighter broth that lets the ingredients speak, Kushiro's need for speed in a fishing town — each can be read as a shape born of what daily life there demanded. The sheer range of these regional differences mirrors the range of the island's own climate and livelihoods.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
もち米とうるち米を食紅でほんのり色づけし、炊きあがりに甘納豆を混ぜ込む赤飯。小豆を炊き込みごま塩で仕上げる全国的な赤飯と違い、甘みのある味が特徴とされる。炊きたての熱で甘納豆のまわりが少しとろけ、その部分だけひときわ甘くなるという。おかずと一緒に食べても違和感のない、ほんのりとした甘さが持ち味とされる。
## どう作るのか
もち米とうるち米を混ぜて食紅で色をつけて炊き、炊き上がった赤飯に甘納豆を混ぜ込むだけ。もともとのレシピではもち米とうるち米を1対1で合わせるとされるが、その割合は好みで変わり、各家庭が独自にアレンジを加えて受け継いでいるという。小豆を煮る手間がいらない分、家庭でも手軽に仕上げられ、忙しい朝でも短時間でつくれるのが受け継がれてきた理由の一つとされる。甘納豆の量や食紅の濃さも、家庭ごとの好みで加減されるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
小豆を炊く手間のかかる赤飯を、忙しい母親でも手軽につくれるようにと考案された簡便な調理法が広まったと伝わる。甘納豆をそのまま使うことで小豆を一から煮る工程を省き、食紅で色だけを整える発想が、北海道独自の赤飯の形をつくったといえる。通年手に入るもち米とうるち米、甘納豆を使うため季節を問わず食べられ、学校給食に出されることもあるという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Glutinous and regular rice are tinted a soft pink with food coloring, then folded together with candied sweet beans once cooked — a sekihan quite unlike the nationwide version, which is cooked with azuki beans and finished plain with sesame salt. This one carries real sweetness. The heat of the freshly cooked rice is said to soften the beans slightly at the edges, leaving those spots especially sweet. The result is mild enough sweetness that it sits comfortably alongside savory side dishes.
## How it's made
Glutinous and regular rice are mixed, tinted with food coloring, and cooked, then candied sweet beans are simply folded into the finished rice. The original recipe is said to call for a one-to-one mix of the two rices, though the ratio shifts by taste, with each household said to carry on its own variation. Skipping the work of simmering azuki beans from scratch makes it quick enough to put together even on a busy morning, which is said to be part of why it stuck. How much candied bean goes in, and how deep the pink runs, is also said to come down to each household's own taste.
## Why it took this shape
The simplified method is said to have spread as a way for a busy mother to make sekihan without the labor of simmering azuki beans from scratch. Using ready-made candied beans instead, and reaching for food coloring just to tint the rice, is the idea said to have shaped this distinctly Hokkaido version of the dish. Since glutinous rice, regular rice, and candied beans are all available year-round, it's eaten in every season, and is said to turn up on school lunch menus too.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
内臓を抜いたイカの胴に、もち米とうるち米を詰めて、醤油と砂糖の煮汁でじっくりと炊き上げる駅弁料理。イカの旨みが染み込んだ米粒は甘辛いタレをまとい、お腹にたまる食べごたえがある。ゲソやたけのこ、しいたけ、グリーンピースなどを刻んで一緒に詰めることもあり、地域では家庭の軽食やおやつ、酒の肴としても親しまれてきたという。
## どう作るのか
ゲソと呼ばれる足の部分を外し、内臓を取り出してきれいに洗った胴に、もち米とうるち米を詰めて楊枝で留める。醤油、砂糖、塩、酒を加えた鍋でじっくりと炊き込む。もち米を詰めすぎると加熱で膨らんで胴が破裂してしまうため、あらかじめ胴に楊枝で数カ所穴をあけておくのがコツと伝わる。煮汁が胴の中までじっくり染み込むよう、弱火で時間をかけて炊き上げるのが持ち味とされる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
第二次世界大戦中、米の統制で不足が深刻化するなか、「少しでも米を節約できる料理」として函館本線森駅の駅弁に考案されたのが始まりと伝わる。当時、道南地域で大量に水揚げされていたイカを使うことで、米の使用量を抑えながらも食べごたえのある一品に仕立てた工夫が読み取れる。列車が到着するたびに買い求める人が絶えない、道南を代表する駅弁として根づいてきたという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
A squid body, cleaned of its innards, is stuffed with a mix of glutinous and regular rice and slow-simmered in a soy-and-sugar broth — a dish born as a station bento. The rice, soaked through with the squid's own savor, comes wrapped in a sweet-salty glaze and makes for a filling meal. Chopped tentacles, bamboo shoot, shiitake, or green peas sometimes go into the stuffing too, and locally it's said to double as a light snack or something to go with a drink.
## How it's made
The tentacles, called geso, are removed, and the cleaned, hollowed-out body is stuffed with glutinous and regular rice and pinned shut with a toothpick. It's then slow-simmered in a pot with soy sauce, sugar, salt, and sake. Overstuff it with glutinous rice and the body can split as it swells with heat, so poking a few small holes in the body beforehand with a toothpick is said to be the trick that prevents it. The gentle, unhurried simmer is said to be what lets the broth work its way all through the body.
## Why it took this shape
During the Second World War, as wartime rice controls made shortages severe, it's said to have been devised as a station bento at Mori Station on the Hakodate Main Line — a dish meant to stretch rice as far as it would go. Using squid, which was landed in huge quantities in the Donan region at the time, is a way of reading the dish's own logic: keep the rice to a minimum while still making something filling. It's said to have become the signature station bento of the Donan region, with buyers lining up every time a train pulls in.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
ぶつ切りにしたサケの身と中骨などのあらを、キャベツやたまねぎ、大根といった野菜と一緒に昆布だしで煮て、味噌で仕立てる鍋。最後にひとふり加える山椒が、魚と味噌の匂いを抑えて香りを引き締めるという。家庭によってはいくらを添えて贅沢に、あるいはバターでこくを足すこともあり、サケの皮に含まれるコラーゲンもたっぷり味わえる一皿とされる。
## どう作るのか
昆布のだし汁に、ぶつ切りにしたサケの身とあらを入れ、野菜と一緒に煮込んで味噌で味をととのえる。あらを使うことで骨まわりの旨みごと汁に溶け出すという。具材はたまねぎ、キャベツ、長ねぎ、大根、しいたけ、豆腐などが一般的だが、加える組み合わせは家庭によってさまざまで、味噌の配合も各家庭の好みに委ねられているという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
石狩川の河口にある石狩地方は、江戸時代からサケ漁が盛んな土地だった。大漁を祝う際、漁師たちがとれたてのサケのぶつ切りやあらを、そのまま味噌汁の鍋に入れてご褒美として食べていたのが始まりと伝わる。骨やあらまで余さず鍋に入れる豪快さは、サケが大量に揚がる漁師町ならではの発想といえ、いまも石狩地方には石狩鍋を出す店がいくつも残っているという。冬に大鍋でぐつぐつと煮て熱いまま食べる、身体を温める鍋料理として定着してきた。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Chunks of salmon along with its trimmings — the backbone and other odd cuts — simmer with cabbage, onion, and daikon in a kelp-based broth, finished with miso. A final pinch of sansho pepper is said to round off the fish and miso smell and sharpen the aroma. Some households add salmon roe for a richer bowl, or a knob of butter for depth, and the dish is said to deliver plenty of the collagen found in salmon skin.
## How it's made
Chunks of salmon and its trimmings go into a kelp broth along with vegetables, then the whole pot is seasoned with miso. Using the trimmings is said to let the savor around the bones dissolve straight into the broth. Onion, cabbage, green onion, daikon, shiitake, and tofu are the common vegetables, though which ones go in — and how strong the miso runs — is said to be left to each household's own taste.
## Why it took this shape
The Ishikari region, at the mouth of the Ishikari River, has been a center of salmon fishing since the Edo period. It's said to have begun when fishermen, celebrating a good catch, dropped chunks and trimmings of freshly caught salmon straight into a pot of miso soup as a reward for the day's work. Putting bones and trimmings into the pot without holding anything back reads as an idea that could only come from a fishing town awash in salmon, and Ishikari is still said to be home to several restaurants serving it today. It's the kind of hot pot meant to be simmered in a big pot and eaten piping hot, to warm the body through a cold winter.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
北海道の方言で「エイ」を意味するカスベを、しょうがと一緒に醤油、砂糖、みりんで煮る冬の料理。軟骨魚のため骨までやわらかく、身から骨まで残すところなく食べられる。冷めると身に含まれるコラーゲンが固まって煮こごりになり、木の芽を添えてそのまま食べても美味とされる。安価で手に入るため、冬の食卓のおかずとしても酒の肴としても親しまれてきたという。
## どう作るのか
カスベをぶつ切りにし、しょうがと一緒に砂糖、醤油、酒、みりんで煮る。よく煮込めば骨まで柔らかく食べられるようになるという。カスベは日が経つと臭みが出やすく鮮度が命とされ、しょうがを加えることでその臭みを抑える効果があると伝わる。冷めて煮こごりになったものは、そのまま酒の肴として食べられることも多い。
## なぜこの形になったのか
調理法が確立していなかった昔、体内でアンモニア臭を発するカスベは臭みが強く敬遠され、食用ではなく肥料として使われていた歴史もあるという。名前の由来も、煮ても焼いても「かす」にしかならない魚だからという説や、アイヌ語の「カシュムベ」に由来するという説など諸説伝わる。臭みを抑える調理法が広まったことで、いまでは冬の家庭料理として好まれるようになったと伝わる。コラーゲンが豊富なことから、近年は美容食としても注目されているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Kasube — the local word for ray or skate — is simmered with ginger in soy sauce, sugar, and mirin, a winter dish. Being cartilaginous, the bones stay soft enough to eat along with the flesh, nothing wasted. Left to cool, the collagen in the meat sets into a jelly, said to be delicious on its own with a sprig of sansho leaf. Being affordable, it's said to have become a familiar winter side dish and something to go with a drink alike.
## How it's made
The ray is cut into chunks and simmered with ginger in sugar, soy sauce, sake, and mirin. Cooked through, even the bones are said to turn soft enough to eat. Kasube is said to develop an odor quickly once caught, so freshness is everything, and ginger is said to help mask that smell. Once cooled into a jelly, it's often eaten just as it is, as an accompaniment to a drink.
## Why it took this shape
Before a way of cooking it had been worked out, kasube — which gives off an ammonia-like smell in the body — is said to have been shunned for its odor, once used as fertilizer rather than food. The name's origin has several tellings too: that boiled or grilled, it was once thought fit for nothing but kasu, or scraps, or that it derives from the Ainu word kashumbe. Once methods for taming the smell spread, it's said to have become a favored winter dish in the home, and its collagen has more recently drawn attention as a beauty food too.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
塩蔵した塩くじらを、大根や豆腐、山菜と一緒に醤油味で煮込む正月料理。何度も温め直して食べるため、一緒に入れる野菜には煮崩れしにくい食材が選ばれるという。くじらから出る旨みと野菜の甘みが溶け合った汁は栄養価が高く、極寒の北海道の冬を乗り切るために欠かせない料理だったと伝わる。一部の地域ではいまも「くじな汁」と呼ばれている。
## どう作るのか
塩くじらの脂身を、豆腐や山菜、大根、ねぎ、しいたけ、里芋などの野菜と合わせて醤油味で煮込む。家庭によっては塩味や味噌味でつくることもあるが、基本は醤油味とされる。かつては晩秋に保存しておいた野菜や、塩漬けにした山菜を塩抜きしてから使っていたが、冷凍技術が発達したいまは使う野菜も家庭によってさまざまという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
江戸後期から明治にかけてニシン漁が盛んだった道南地域では、ニシンを岸へ追い込んでくれる鯨は縁起の良い生き物として崇められていたと伝わる。初春から始まるニシン漁の豊漁を願い、正月にこの汁を食べる習いが根づいたという。北海道では貴重なタンパク源として塩くじらを保存食にしていた歴史もあり、厳しい冬を乗り切るための栄養と、豊漁への願いが一つの椀に重なっている料理といえる。大物であるくじらの姿にあやかり、年越しに食べる地域もあるという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Salted whale meat is simmered with daikon, tofu, and mountain vegetables in a soy-seasoned broth — a New Year dish. Because it's reheated and eaten again and again, the vegetables chosen for it are ones that hold their shape rather than falling apart. The broth, rich with the whale's savor melted into the vegetables' sweetness, is said to have been a nutrient-dense dish essential to getting through Hokkaido's bitter winters. In some areas it's still called "kujina-jiru" today.
## How it's made
Fatty cuts of salted whale are simmered in a soy-seasoned broth with tofu, mountain vegetables, daikon, green onion, shiitake, and taro. Some households make it with salt or miso instead, though soy sauce is said to be the standard. Vegetables once meant late-autumn stores or salt-preserved wild greens, soaked to remove the salt before use; now that freezing is common, what goes in varies by household.
## Why it took this shape
In the Donan region, where herring fishing thrived from the late Edo period into the Meiji era, whales — said to drive herring in toward shore — were revered as auspicious creatures. Eating this soup at New Year, in hope of a good herring catch once the season opened in early spring, is said to be how the custom took hold. Hokkaido also has a history of salting whale meat as a preserved food, a valuable source of protein — so in one bowl sit both the nutrition needed to survive a hard winter and a wish for a good catch to come. Some places are said to eat it at year's end too, drawing on the whale's own great size as a good omen.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
サケやマスを凍らせたまま、解凍せずに薄く切って食べる刺身。口に入れた瞬間の凍った食感と、そこからじわりと溶けていく味わいの変化が持ち味とされる。わさび醤油で食べるのが一般的だが、レモンを絞ったり大根おろしを添えたりと食べ方はさまざま。ヒメマスやイカなど、ほかの魚介を凍らせたまま薄切りにしたものを指すこともあるという。
## どう作るのか
サケやマスを雪に埋めるなどして凍らせ、凍ったまま薄く切り分けて刺身にする。凍らせることで身に潜む寄生虫を死滅させる効果もあるとされ、保存と安全の両方を兼ねた調理法といえる。地域や家庭によっては、軽くあぶってから食べたり、塩を振って食べたりと味わい方に幅があり、いくらと生サケを漬けてから凍らせる「ルイベ漬け」といった派生も伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
アイヌ発祥の料理と伝わる。寒さの厳しい冬に備え、貴重なタンパク源だったサケを雪に埋めて凍らせて保存し、そのまま薄く切って食べたのが始まりとされる。名前もアイヌ語の「溶ける」を意味する「ル」と「食料」を意味する「イペ」を合わせた言葉が語源といわれる。厳寒の気候そのものが天然の冷凍庫となり、保存と食感という二つの効果を一度に生んだ料理と読み解ける。いまでは全国的にも知られ、道内では豚肉を使う変わり種のルイベもつくられているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Salmon or trout is frozen and sliced thin while still frozen, eaten as sashimi without thawing. The appeal is said to lie in that first icy bite giving way, moment by moment, to a slow melt in the mouth. Wasabi and soy sauce is the usual way to eat it, though a squeeze of lemon or a side of grated daikon are common too. The word can also cover other seafood — kokanee salmon, squid — sliced the same way while still frozen.
## How it's made
Salmon or trout is frozen, often by burying it in snow, then sliced thin while it's still frozen solid. Freezing is also said to kill off any parasites hiding in the flesh, making the method one that serves preservation and safety at once. How it's eaten varies — lightly seared, or simply salted — and a variant called ruibe-zuke, where raw salmon and roe are marinated before freezing, is also passed down.
## Why it took this shape
It's said to be a dish of Ainu origin. Salmon, a vital source of protein, was frozen by burying it in snow to see through the harsh cold of winter, and slicing it thin straight from that frozen state is said to be how this began. The name itself is said to come from Ainu words — ru, meaning "to melt," and ipe, meaning "food." The bitter cold climate itself became a natural freezer, and the dish can be read as one that got both preservation and a particular texture out of that single fact. It's known nationwide today, and on the island a variant made with pork instead of fish is also said to be made.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
塩漬けにしたサケやタラ、ニシンと、大根やじゃがいもなどの野菜を一緒に煮て、魚の塩分だけで味を調えるシンプルな汁物。同じサケを使う石狩鍋と混同されがちだが、味噌仕立てで生のサケを使う石狩鍋に対し、三平汁は主に塩漬けの魚を使うのが違いとされる。魚の頭や骨も一緒に煮込むことで、より一層旨みが増すといい、寒い冬に身体を芯から温めてくれる汁物として親しまれている。
## どう作るのか
昆布で出汁をとったあと、魚の塩引きや糠漬けを大根や人参、長ねぎ、じゃがいもなどの野菜と一緒に煮る。使う魚や味付けは地域によって幅があり、道央・道東では塩ザケ、道北では塩ダラも使われるという。檜山地方では塩だけで仕立てる「塩三平」と、味噌で仕立てる「味噌三平」の両方が伝わり、家庭ごとに味付けも具材もさまざまという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
名前の由来には諸説あり、松前藩の藩主が狩りの際に漁師の家であり合わせの汁を食べて気に入ったためという言い伝えや、有田焼の深皿「三平皿」に盛ったことに由来するという説が伝わる。江戸時代後期の紀行文「東遊記」にすでにその記述が残るとされ、寒さの厳しい冬に魚の塩分だけで身体を温める、道内の暮らしに根ざした汁物として受け継がれてきたと読み解ける。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Salted salmon, cod, or herring simmers with daikon, potato, and other vegetables in a simple broth seasoned by nothing but the fish's own salt. It's often confused with ishikari-nabe, which also uses salmon, but the two differ in that ishikari-nabe is miso-seasoned and uses raw salmon, while sampei-jiru is built mainly on salted fish. Simmering the fish heads and bones along with everything else is said to deepen the savor further, and it's cherished as a soup that warms the body through on a cold winter's day.
## How it's made
After a kelp stock is drawn, salted or rice-bran-cured fish simmers with daikon, carrot, green onion, and potato. Which fish is used and how it's seasoned varies by region — salted salmon in central and eastern Hokkaido, salted cod as well in the north. In the Hiyama region, both a salt-only version, shio-sanpei, and a miso version, miso-sanpei, are said to be passed down, with the seasoning and ingredients otherwise left up to each household.
## Why it took this shape
The name's origin carries more than one telling — a story that the lord of the Matsumae domain, out hunting, ate a soup thrown together from whatever a fisherman's household had on hand and took a liking to it, or that it comes from the deep Arita-ware dish, the sanpei-zara, it was once served in. A record of it is said to already appear in the late-Edo-period travelogue Toyuki. It can be read as a broth rooted in the everyday life of the island — warming the body through the harsh cold of winter on nothing but the salt already in the fish.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
太平洋沿岸のごく限られた河川にしか遡上しない、日本固有種のシシャモを素焼きにし、醤油とみりん、砂糖でじっくりと煮含める料理。骨まで丸ごと食べられ、卵を抱えた子持ちの雌がとりわけ美味とされる。全国に流通するシシャモの多くは大西洋でとれる輸入の「カラフトシシャモ」で、北海道でとれる本来のシシャモはごくわずかしか出回らないという。
## どう作るのか
シシャモを素焼きにしたあと、鍋に入れて10分ほど煮てから、砂糖、みりん、醤油を加え、煮汁がなくなるまでじっくり煮詰める。好みで根しょうがの千切りを加えることもあるという。素焼きにしてから煮る二段構えの調理で、身の香ばしさを保ちながら味を含ませているとされる。骨まで柔らかく食べられるよう、火加減を見ながらじっくり仕上げるのがコツと伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
シシャモは川で生まれて海で育つ回遊魚で、10月中旬から11月の晩秋にかけて群れで川を遡上し、川底で産卵する。この限られた時季にしか遡上しないことが、北海道でとれる本来のシシャモの希少さにつながっていると伝わる。アイヌの人々にとって冬を越す貴重な食材だったといい、漢字で「柳葉魚」と書くのも、アイヌの神が柳の葉からシシャモをつくったという逸話に基づくとされる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Shishamo, a fish found only in a handful of rivers along the Pacific coast and native to Japan, is grilled plain, then slow-simmered in soy sauce, mirin, and sugar. Bones and all, the whole fish is eaten, and the roe-bearing females are said to be the best of all. Most shishamo sold nationwide are actually imported capelin from the Atlantic, and the true, Hokkaido-caught fish is said to reach the market only in small numbers.
## How it's made
The fish is grilled plain first, then simmered in a pot for about ten minutes before sugar, mirin, and soy sauce are added and it's reduced slowly until the liquid is gone. Some add julienned ginger root to taste. Grilling before simmering is a two-step approach said to keep the fish's own toastiness while letting the seasoning soak in. Watching the heat carefully through that slow simmer is said to be the trick that lets the bones turn soft enough to eat.
## Why it took this shape
Shishamo is a migratory fish, born in rivers and raised at sea, that returns upstream in schools from mid-October through late November to spawn on the riverbed. This narrow window is said to be exactly why the true, Hokkaido-caught fish stays so scarce. It's said to have been a vital food for the Ainu to see through winter, and even its kanji, meaning "willow-leaf fish," is said to come from a tale that an Ainu deity fashioned the fish from a willow leaf.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
マダラやスケソウダラの白子を丸ごと昆布だしに入れ、味噌を溶いただけのシンプルな汁物。北海道では白子を「たち」と呼び、マダラのものは「真だち」、スケソウダラのものは「すけだち」と呼んで区別するという。真だちは特に高級品として扱われ、なめらかな舌ざわりとほのかな磯の香りが冬の食卓を彩ると伝わる。すけだちは晩秋ごろから店頭に並び、手ごろな価格で楽しめるという。
## どう作るのか
生の白子を塩でしっかりと洗って臭みを取り、昆布だしでさっと湯がいてから味噌を溶き入れる。「たち」と長ねぎだけのシンプルな一杯が基本だが、大根や人参、白菜、たまねぎ、豆腐を加えて具だくさんにすることもあるという。煮すぎると崩れてしまうため、火を通しすぎないのがコツとされ、季節によって加える具材を変える家庭も多いという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
冷水性のマダラは生息に適した水温が2度から4度と低く、そのため海水温の低い北海道周辺に多く分布し、全国トップクラスの漁獲量を誇るとされる。夏から秋にかけて回遊するスケソウダラも道内ほぼ全域で獲れる。「鱈」の字が魚偏に雪と書くように、雪の降る寒い季節こそが旬とされ、真だちは1月から2月ごろに特に味が良いとされる、冬の海の恵みそのものを映した料理といえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
The milt of Pacific cod or walleye pollock goes whole into a kelp broth, with just miso stirred in — about as simple as a soup gets. In Hokkaido, milt is called "tachi," with Pacific cod's called "ma-dachi" and walleye pollock's "suke-dachi" to tell them apart. Ma-dachi in particular is treated as a delicacy, its smooth texture and faint brine-like aroma said to color the winter table. Suke-dachi appears in shops from around late autumn, said to be the more affordable of the two.
## How it's made
Raw milt is thoroughly rinsed in salt to remove any odor, briefly blanched in kelp broth, then miso is stirred in. The simplest version is just the milt and green onion, though daikon, carrot, napa cabbage, onion, or tofu are sometimes added for a heartier bowl. Cooked too long it falls apart, so the trick is said to be not overdoing the heat, and many households are said to vary what goes in with the season.
## Why it took this shape
Pacific cod is a cold-water fish that lives best at 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, so it's found in abundance around Hokkaido's cold coastal waters, said to account for one of the largest catches nationwide. Walleye pollock, which migrates from summer into autumn, is also caught across nearly the whole island. The kanji for "tara" (cod) combines "fish" with "snow," fitting for a fish whose season is the cold, snowy months, with ma-dachi said to taste best from around January into February — a dish that mirrors the winter sea itself.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
カニを昆布だしでじっくり煮て味噌で仕立て、豆腐と長ねぎを加える汁物。とりわけ根室地方でとれる花咲ガニが使われることで知られる。かご漁で獲られ、漁期は7月中旬から9月下旬とごく短い希少な蟹で、生きているうちは色の濃い茶褐色だが、茹でると鮮やかな朱色に染まるという。カニから出る出汁の旨みが汁全体に広がる、素材の力で勝負する一杯とされる。
## どう作るのか
カニと好みの野菜を昆布だしでじっくり煮込み、味噌で味付けして、最後に豆腐と長ねぎを加えるだけのつくり方。花咲ガニのほか、毛ガニやタラバガニ、ズワイガニなど北海道でとれる別の蟹を使うこともある。野菜を入れずにカニ本来の出汁と旨みだけを味わう食べ方をする家庭もあるといい、手軽さと旨みの強さを両立させた家庭料理として根づいているという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
根室地方の漁師料理として食べられてきたと伝わる。名前の由来は、箸でカニの脚をつついて身を取り出す仕草が、鉄砲に弾を込める動きに似ることからと伝わる。花咲ガニは根室半島の海域でのみ獲れる希少な蟹で、資源保護のためサイズ選別も行われているという。狭い漁場と短い漁期に支えられた希少な食材が、土地の名を冠した汁物として受け継がれてきたといえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Crab simmers slowly in a kelp broth seasoned with miso, with tofu and green onion added at the end. It's especially known for using hanasaki crab, caught off the Nemuro region — a scarce crab taken only by trap fishing in a short season running from mid-July to late September, dark brown while alive but said to turn a vivid vermilion once boiled. The broth carries the crab's own savor through the whole bowl — a soup that lets the ingredient do the work.
## How it's made
Crab and whatever vegetables are on hand simmer slowly in a kelp broth, seasoned with miso, with tofu and green onion stirred in at the end. Besides hanasaki crab, other Hokkaido crabs — snow crab, red king crab, horsehair crab — are sometimes used instead. Some households skip the vegetables entirely, wanting nothing but the crab's own broth and savor — a home-style dish said to be prized for pairing that ease with real depth of flavor.
## Why it took this shape
It's said to have been eaten as a fisherman's dish in the Nemuro region. The name is said to come from the way chopsticks poke at a crab leg to pull out the meat, a motion likened to loading a musket. Hanasaki crab is caught only in the waters off the Nemuro Peninsula, a scarce catch further limited by size selection to protect the resource. A rare ingredient, bound to one small fishing ground and one short season, carried down as a soup that still bears the region's own name.
